hints: Split what you see in Fig. 6.1 into two separate traits - fur length and fur colour pattern - and work out for each trait whether the visible form could hide a recessive allele.
Remember the colour hierarchy is B dominant to b^h dominant to b, so think which two combinations at the B locus both look Himalayan but differ in the hidden allele.
walkthrough:
Decode the short fur phenotype**
Short fur is dominant, controlled by A dominant to a. A rabbit that looks short can be homozygous dominant AA or heterozygous Aa. Both hide no long-fur appearance, but the Aa form carries the hidden a allele.

Decode the Himalayan phenotype**
Himalayan is the middle allele in the series: B > b^h > b. To look Himalayan the rabbit must have at least one b^h and no B, because any B would give all-black fur. That leaves two possibilities: $b^hb^h$ or $b^hb$. The $b^hb$ form carries the hidden white albino allele b.

Combine the two loci**
Length and colour are independent, so combine 2 length options with 2 colour options to give 2 x 2 = 4 genotypes: $AAb^hb^h$, $Aab^hb^h$, $AAb^hb$, $Aab^hb$.

hints: Breeding true means no hidden recessive alleles can be passed on, so think which visible trait at each locus can only be produced by one genotype - the double recessive form.
walkthrough:
What breeding true really means**
If mating two identical-looking rabbits always gives identical offspring, both parents must be homozygous at both loci. Any heterozygote like Aa or $b^hb$ would sometimes pass the hidden allele and produce a different phenotype in the offspring.

Find the only double homozygous recessive**
Long fur is recessive so must be aa. White albino is the bottom recessive so must be bb. Only the long white albino rabbit is aabb and therefore can never carry a hidden A, B or $b^h$ allele.
Final answer: long, white fur all over body (albino).

hints: Start from the two original homozygous parents - work out what genotype a long all-black rabbit and a short all-white rabbit must each have if they are homozygous at both loci.
Think what allele each P parent can give to the F1, and why all F1 look short black even though they receive one allele from each contrasting parent.
When the F1 double heterozygotes make gametes, list all four combinations of one length allele with one colour allele.
Picture a 4 x 4 Punnett square and recall how to group the 16 genotypes by whether they contain at least one A and at least one B.
Count how many squares fall into short black, long black, short white and long white to get the classic dihybrid ratio.
walkthrough:
Work out the P parents and F1**
Long is aa and all-black homozygous is BB, so parent 1 is aaBB. Short homozygous is AA and white homozygous is bb, so parent 2 is AAbb. Each gives only one gamete type: aB and Ab. All F1 receive AaBb and look short black because A dominates a and B dominates b.

List the F1 gametes**
Because the loci are on separate chromosomes, each F1 makes four gamete types in equal numbers: AB, Ab, aB, ab. Both male and female F1 parents make the same set.

Build the F2 Punnett square**
Draw a 4 x 4 grid with male gametes on one side and female gametes on the other. Filling all 16 boxes gives the full genotype set: 1 AABB, 2 AABb, 2 AaBB, 4 AaBb, 1 AAbb, 2 Aabb, 1 aaBB, 2 aaBb, 1 aabb and the remaining AaBb combinations.

Translate genotypes to phenotypes**
Any genotype with A_ and B_ is short black. Any with aa and B_ is long black. Any with A_ and bb is short white. Only aabb is long white. Counting boxes gives 9 short black : 3 long black : 3 short white : 1 long white.

Final answer: F1 genotypes: $AaBb \times AaBb$. gametes: $AB, Ab, aB, ab$ and $AB, Ab, aB, ab$. F2 genotypes: 16-combination Punnett square giving $AABB, AABb, AaBB, AaBb, AABb, AAbb, AaBb, Aabb, AaBB, AaBb, aaBB, aaBb, AaBb, Aabb, aaBb, aabb$. F2 phenotypes ratio: 9 short black : 3 black long : 3 short white : 1 white long.

hints: Recall where the two loci are located in this rabbit and what that tells you about linkage.
Picture what happens to pairs of homologous chromosomes on the equator during the first division of meiosis.
Link random orientation to the number of different gamete types and why parental combinations are broken up.
walkthrough:
Separate chromosomes means no linkage**
The A/a locus and B/b locus are on different chromosomes, so they cannot travel together as a linked block. They behave as completely separate units through meiosis.

Random orientation in metaphase I**
In metaphase I homologous pairs line up as bivalents on the equator. Which way round each bivalent faces - which homologue points to which pole - is random and independent of all other bivalents. So the chromosome carrying A or a lines up independently of the chromosome carrying B or b.

New allele combinations**
That independent orientation produces four genetically different gametes - AB, Ab, aB, ab - in equal numbers. It shuffles maternal and paternal alleles so offspring show new combinations, not just the parental types. This is independent assortment.

Final answer: Genes on separate chromosomes are not linked. Each bivalent / pair of homologous chromosomes orients randomly / independently at the equator in metaphase I of meiosis, giving four different gamete combinations and parental allele combinations are not preserved.

hints: Add up all the observed rabbits to get the total, then split that total in the 9:3:3:1 ratio predicted for independent assortment.
walkthrough:
Use the total and the 9:3:3:1 prediction**
Total observed $= 25 + 11 + 8 + 4 = 48$. For independent assortment expect $9/16$, $3/16$, $3/16$, $1/16$ of 48. That is $27$ short black, $9$ long black, $9$ short white and $3$ long white. These match the $(O-E)^2$ values given: e.g. $(25-27)^2 = 4$.
Final answer: Total = 48. Expected: short black 27, long black 9, short white 9, long white 3.

walkthrough:
Add the four components**
$\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O-E)^2}{E}$. Adding the column: $0.148 + 0.444 + 0.111 + 0.333 = 1.036$.
